text: Certificates. The following is formally verified in Lean, with native_decide as explained below. Independently of the lattice computation, each of the \(3400\) groups (understood as the group defined by its ANUPQ pc presentation on \(g_0,\dots,g_9\)) comes with a finite module \(V=\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/2^{a_i}\) and matrices for the action of the \(g_k\) (found from a truncated Magnus algebra mod \(2^E\); only the check matters). Lean checks that the presentation has pc shape, that the matrices are well defined and invertible on \(V\) and satisfy the pc relations, that every product \((g_{k_1}-1)\cdots(g_{k_4}-1)\) acts as \(0\) on \(V\) (checked on spanning sets: starting from the standard generators of \(V\), the images under the \(g_k-1\) are reduced to a spanning set at each depth, and none is left at depth \(4\); a lemma proved in Lean and checked by the kernel shows that this suffices), and that the \(2^{10}\) normal words act by distinct operators. A theorem proved in Lean and checked by the kernel turns a passing check into a faithful representation whose linear extension kills \(\Delta^4\), so \(D_4(Q)=D_5(Q)=1\) and \(|Q|=2^{10}\) (D_four_cand, card_cand; directory GroupDimension/Cert1024/). The \(3400\) checks themselves run as compiled code (native_decide, \(34\) calls), not in the kernel, so they trust the Lean compiler. With GAP, the relations of every presentation were verified in the corresponding ANUPQ group, so by \(|Q|=2^{10}\) the presented group is that group. The completeness of the list of \(3400\) rests on Lemma 5.2(d), which is formally verified, and on the ANUPQ search, a computation that is not certified.

Checks of the order-\(2^{10}\) search. The same pipeline at orders \(2^6,\dots,2^9\) (parents from SmallGroups of half the order) was compared with a direct pass over SmallGroups of that order: the numbers of class-\(3\) groups with \(|P_c|=2\) and \(2\)-class \(\ge4\) (\(3\), \(27\), \(320\), \(4185\)), of those with cyclic centre, and of the candidates (\(3\), \(11\), \(64\), \(308\)) agree, also rank by rank. A second lattice method (the truncated Magnus algebra of §7, item 1, run on a pc-presentation, so independent of the multiplication table) gives the same answer on \(3391\) of the \(3400\) candidates. The search took \(62.9\) CPU-hours in GAP and the lattices \(21.3\) CPU-hours. The code and the per-chunk and per-candidate tables are in compute/pq1024.

Theorem (Computer-assisted). • \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(2\)-subgroup has order at most \(2^{10}\); in particular for every group of order less than \(2048\). • \(D_n(G)=\gamma_n(G)\) for all \(n\) and every finite group \(G\) of order less than \(512\). • \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) has no \(3\)-torsion for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(3\)-subgroup has order at most \(3^7\); in fact \(D_5(Q)=\gamma_5(Q)\) for every \(3\)-group \(Q\) of order at most \(3^7\). (Extended to \(3^9\) in Theorem 6.14.)

Proof. (1) is Remark 2.3 with Propositions 5.1 and 5.3: every metabelian \(2\)-group of class \(3\) and order \(\le 2^{10}\) is covered (orders \(\le2^8\) by the lattice for all groups, \(2^9\) by the sieve and the lattice, \(2^{10}\) by Lemma 5.2, ANUPQ and the lattice). For (2) and (3): a finite nilpotent group is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups and \(D_n\), \(\gamma_n\) respect direct products, and for non-nilpotent finite \(G\) one reduces to the nilpotent quotients \(G/\gamma_m(G)\) (this is standard, see [MP09]); groups of order \(<512\) have \(2\)-part \(\le2^8\), \(3\)-part \(\le3^5\) and \(p\)-part \(\le p^3\) for \(p\ge5\), where class \(\le2\) makes everything trivial. For the \(3\)-part in (3): if \(Q\) is a \(3\)-group of order \(\le3^7\), then \(Q/\gamma_5(Q)\) has class \(\le4\) and order \(\le3^7\), hence is metabelian (class \(\le3\) always is, Remark 2.2; class \(4\) by Proposition 5.1), and Gupta–Tahara [GT85, Thm. 3.2(c)] (\(D_{p+2}=\gamma_{p+2}\) for finitely generated metabelian \(p\)-groups, \(p\) odd) gives \(D_5(Q/\gamma_5)=1\), i.e. \(D_5(Q)\subseteq\gamma_5(Q)\). For the \(1202\) candidates of order \(3^7\) this gives \(D_5=\gamma_5\) by a theorem, independently of item (3) of Proposition 5.1, where \(D_n=\gamma_n\) for all \(n\) was computed for each of them (for all \(n\) this also follows from [Gup91], as they are metabelian). The reduction for non-nilpotent groups in (2)–(3) is standard, and we do not write it out.

Observations. In every group of class \(c\) computed, \(D_{c+1}=1\) and \(D_k=\gamma_k\) at each step. For metabelian groups of class \(3\) the Jennings sieve removes almost everything (orders \(64\), \(128\), \(256\), \(512\): \(111/114\), \(1116/1137\), \(21\,105/21\,325\), \(1\,584\,597/1\,587\,389\)), and the survivors have \(D_4=1\) already. For \(3\)-groups of class \(4\) the sieve removes little (\(9/71\) at order \(729\), \(107/1309\) at order \(2187\)). Computing time: about \(3.6\) hours wall clock, about \(30\)–\(40\) CPU-hours.

Remark (pruning the generation tree). Let \(Q\) be a finite \(2\)-group of class \(3\) with cyclic centre, \(d=d(Q)\), \(C=C_Q(\gamma_2(Q))\), \(X=\gamma_2(Q)/(\gamma_2(Q)\cap Z(Q))\). The commutator map \(X\times Q/C\to\gamma_3(Q)\) is a non-degenerate bilinear pairing into the cyclic group \(\gamma_3(Q)\le Z(Q)\); hence \(X\cong Q/C\), a quotient of \(Q_{ab}\), and \(X\) has rank \(\le\min(d,d(d-1)/2)\). If \(|\gamma_3(Q)|=2^e\), then \(Q_{ab}\) has two invariants \(\ge 2^e\) (the map \((u,v)\mapsto[u,v,z]\) factors through \(\Lambda^2Q_{ab}\)) and \(X\) has an element of order \(\ge 2^e\). For a minimal counterexample \(Q\) (Lemma 5.2) with central involution \(n\) this gives conditions on every quotient \(V=Q/N\) with \(N\le\Phi(Q)\) (with \(n\in N\le\Phi(Q)\) for the second), which pass to further quotients and so may be used to cut whole subtrees of the \(p\)-group generation tree: (i) there is a cyclic \(K\), \(\gamma_3(V)\le K\le\gamma_2(V)\cap Z(V)\), with \(\mathrm{rk}(\gamma_2(V)/K)\le\min(d,d(d-1)/2)\); (ii) for such a \(K\), \(|Q|\ge 2|K|\,|A\vee B\vee E_1|\,|A\vee V_{ab}\vee E_2|\), where \(A=\gamma_2(V)/K\), \(B=V/C_V(\gamma_2(V))\), \(E_1=\mathbb{Z}/2^{e_V+1}\), \(E_2=E_1^2\), \(2^{e_V}=|\gamma_3(V)|\), and \(\vee\) is the componentwise maximum of abelian invariants. In particular every such \(V\) of class \(3\) has \(d+4e_V+2\le\log_2|Q|\). These conditions are proved by hand; the proofs are in compute/pq2048/README.md. Condition (i) is vacuous for \(d\le3\) and below order \(2^{2d+1}\); condition (ii) is the one that cuts.

Order \(2^{11}\), ranks \(2\)–\(7\). At order \(2^{11}\) the same argument needs as parents the groups of order \(2^{10}\) of class \(\le3\) with cyclic \(\gamma_3\); they are not in SmallGroups, and their number is estimated at \(0.5\)–\(1.1\cdot10^9\). Remark 5.5 cuts whole subtrees without losing a candidate (checked: the same \(3\), \(11\), \(64\), \(308\) candidates at orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\)) and leaves, by a sample, \(10^5\)–\(2\cdot10^6\) parents; without rules (A), (B), (T) below, generating them would take an estimated \(100\) CPU-days, mostly at rank \(5\). Ranks \(2\)–\(7\) have been run through to order \(2^{11}\): \(17\), \(586\), \(52\,568\), \(824\), \(13\) and \(9\) candidates (at ranks \(5\) and \(6\) after rule (T) below), all with \(D_4=D_5=1\) by computation (with the second lattice method described after Proposition 5.3). For rank \(4\) the walk passes through \(2\,756\) candidates at order \(2^{10}\), exactly the rank-\(4\) count of Proposition 5.3; it kept \(52\,181\) parents of order \(2^{10}\) and cut \(9\,937\), \(136\,127\), \(946\,663\) vertices at orders \(2^8\), \(2^9\), \(2^{10}\) (code: compute/pq2048). The pruned search used there was checked at order \(2^{10}\), where it reproduces the \(3400\) candidates of Proposition 5.3 exactly, rank by rank, while keeping \(4.2\%\) of the parents. Ranks \(5\) and \(6\) used, on top of Remark 5.5, three more rules, each proved by hand; the proofs and references are in compute/pq2048/README.md. (A) A vertex of order \(2^9\), \(2\)-class \(2\) and elementary abelianization is not expanded: it is not a parent, its steps \(\ge2\) go past order \(2^{10}\), and its step-\(1\) descendants all have class \(3\) and fail the bound of Remark 5.5(ii). (B) The step-\(1\) descendants of class \(3\) of a vertex of order \(2^9\) and \(2\)-class \(2\) whose abelianization has fewer than two invariants \(\ge4\) are dropped, as they fail the same bound. (T) A leaf of order \(2^{10}\) whose abelianization has at most one invariant \(\ge4\) is dropped: a candidate \(Q\) above it has the same abelianization, so \(D_4(Q)=\gamma_4(Q)=1\) by Tahara's Corollary 19 [Tah77a, p. 125] (for a \(2\)-group of class \(3\) whose abelianization has at most one cyclic factor of order \(\ge4\), \(D_4=\gamma_4\); Tahara attributes it to Passi [Pas79, Thm. 10.1]) and hence \(D_5(Q)=1\). Rules (A) and (B) lose no candidate. Rule (T) does drop candidates, but only ones with \(D_5=1\), so the rank-\(5\) and rank-\(6\) counts above are of the candidates left after it; a rank-\(6\) run that applied (T) to only part of its pieces kept \(469\) candidates, all with \(D_4=D_5=1\) by computation. These two ranks were run with ANUPQ with the fixes of the audit mentioned in the proof of Theorem 6.14, and with automorphism groups not computed for descendants that are leaves (an option proposed upstream as gap-packages/anupq#124; on \(283\) test groups this version gives the same \(35\,213\) descendants as without the option). Ranks \(2\)–\(4\) and \(7\), like the order-\(2^{10}\) search of Proposition 5.3, were first run with ANUPQ before those fixes (two of the fixed defects can change the descendants) and then repeated with the same fixed build: the results agree exactly, namely the results of all \(858\) pieces of the search and the \(3400\) candidates with their lattice answers at order \(2^{10}\), and the candidates of ranks \(2\)–\(4\) and \(7\) at order \(2^{11}\); so does the direct generation at rank \(8\) described after Proposition 5.7. For rank \(5\) the walk passes through \(319\) candidates at order \(2^{10}\), and for rank \(6\) through \(9\), again exactly the counts of Proposition 5.3; rank \(5\) kept \(206\,519\) parents of order \(2^{10}\). The tree searches took about \(15\) CPU-hours at rank \(4\) and \(83\) at rank \(5\). At rank \(7\) the unmodified ANUPQ fails with an integer overflow on the step-\(2\) descendants of \((\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\); these are the \(1\,112\) groups of order \(2^9\), rank \(7\) and \(2\)-class \(2\), a contiguous block of SmallGroups (by SmallGroupsInformation), and the walk starts from them. Ranks \(\ge8\) need no search (Proposition 5.7 below); so order \(2^{11}\) is settled (Proposition 5.10).

Order \(2^{11}\), rank \(\ge8\). Call a \(2\)-group \(Q\) a candidate if it has class \(3\), cyclic centre with involution \(n\in\gamma_3(Q)\cap M_5(Q)\), and \(2\)-class \(c\ge4\) with \(P_c(Q)=\langle n\rangle\). By Lemma 5.2 and Proposition 5.3, a \(2\)-group of order \(2^{11}\) and class \(3\) with \(D_5\ne1\) is a candidate (its quotients by central subgroups of order \(2\) have order \(2^{10}\) and class \(\le3\)).
Lemma. There is no candidate \(Q\) of order \(2^{11}\) with \(Q/P_3(Q)\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\).
Proof. (The lemma is also formally verified, §4.)

(3) \(M_5(Q)=\prod_{i2^j\ge5}\gamma_i^{2^j}=Q^8\gamma_2^4\gamma_3^2=Q^8\), since \(\gamma_4=1\), \(|\gamma_2|=4\) and \(|\gamma_3|=2\). So \(x^4\) is central. (7) Then \(\gamma_2=\langle x^4angle\le Z(Q)\) and \(\gamma_3=[\gamma_2,Q]=1\), contradicting class \(3\).

Proposition. \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of order \(2^{11}\), class \(3\) and rank \(d(Q)\ge8\). More generally, every candidate \(Q\) has \(|\Phi(Q)|\ge16\), that is, \(d(Q)\le\log_2|Q|-4\).

Proof. (The second statement is proved by hand and is also formally verified, and so is the deduction of the first statement from the second and Proposition 5.3, see §4; through Proposition 5.3 the first statement is computer-assisted.)

The first statement follows from the second: a counterexample would be a candidate (see above) with \(|\Phi(Q)|=2^{11-d}\le8\). Let \(Q\) be a candidate with \(|\Phi(Q)|\le8\). The series \(P_i\) decreases strictly until it reaches \(1\) (if \(P_{i+1}=P_i\), it is constant from \(i\) on), and \(\Phi(Q)=P_2\) (Burnside); since \(c\ge4\), \(P_2\supsetneq P_3\supsetneq P_4\supseteq P_c=\langle n\rangle\) gives \(|P_2|=8\), \(|P_3|=4\) and \(P_4=\langle n\rangle\). Also \(\gamma_2\le P_2\), \(\gamma_3\le P_3\), and \(\gamma_3\) is central since \(\gamma_4=1\); so \([u^m,g]=[u,g]^m\) for \(u\in\gamma_2\), \(g\in Q\), and \(\gamma_3\) is generated by the \([u,g]\). As in step (2) of the proof of Lemma 5.6, \(\gamma_3\ne1\) and \(\gamma_3\ne\gamma_2\), so \(|\gamma_2|\ge4\). Since \(\gamma_4=1\), \(M_5(Q)=Q^8\gamma_2^4\gamma_3^2\), and the generators \(x^8\), \(y^4\) (\(y\in\gamma_2\le P_2\)) and \(z^2\) (\(z\in\gamma_3\le P_3\)) of the three factors lie in \(P_4=\{1,n\}\). As \(n\in M_5(Q)\), one of them equals \(n\).

(a) \(z^2=n\) for some \(z\in\gamma_3\). Then \(z\) has order \(4\), so \(\gamma_3=P_3=\langle z\rangle\) is central. For \(u\in\gamma_2\) and \(g\in Q\) we have \(u^2\in P_3\), hence \([u,g]^2=[u^2,g]=1\) and \([u,g]\in\langle z^2\rangle=\langle n\rangle\). So \(\gamma_3\le\langle n\rangle\), contradicting \(z^2=n\ne1\).

(b) \(y^4=n\) for some \(y\in\gamma_2\). Then \(y\) has order \(8\), so \(\gamma_2=P_2=\langle y\rangle\) and \(P_3=\langle y^2\rangle\). For \(g\in Q\), \([y,g]^2=[y^2,g]\in[P_3,Q]\le P_4=\langle n\rangle\). If \([y,g]^2=n\), then \([y,g]\in\gamma_3\) has order \(4\), so \(\langle[y,g]\rangle=P_3\ni y^2\), and \(y^2\in\gamma_3\) is central: \([y^2,g]=1\), a contradiction. Hence \([y,g]^2=1\), that is, \([y,g]\in\langle y^4\rangle=\langle n\rangle\), and \(\gamma_3\), generated by the \([y^m,g]=[y,g]^m\), lies in \(\langle n\rangle\). Now let \(g,h\in Q\). Since \(g^2\in P_2=\gamma_2\), we have \([g^2,h]\in\gamma_3\), and \([g^2,h]\equiv[g,h]^2\pmod{\gamma_3}\); so \([g,h]^2\in\gamma_3\le\langle n\rangle\), \([g,h]^4=1\) and \([g,h]\in\langle y^2\rangle\). Then \(\gamma_2\le\langle y^2\rangle\) has order \(\le4\), a contradiction.

(c) \(x^8=n\) for some \(x\in Q\). Then \(x^2\in P_2\) has order \(8\), so \(P_2=\langle x^2\rangle\) is cyclic, and \(\gamma_2\le P_2\) has order \(4\) or \(8\). If \(|\gamma_2|=8\), then \(\gamma_2=P_2\ni x^2\) and \((x^2)^4=n\), which is case (b). If \(|\gamma_2|=4\), then \(\gamma_2=\langle x^4\rangle=P_3\), and steps (2)–(7) of the proof of Lemma 5.6 give a contradiction: they use \(Q/P_3(Q)\) only through \(\gamma_2\le P_3\), \(|P_3|=4\), \(P_4=\langle n\rangle\) and \(Q^4\le P_3\), which holds in every group (\(x^4=(x^2)^2\) with \(x^2\in P_2\)).

The bound is sharp at both searched orders: the candidates of order \(2^{10}\) have rank \(\le6\), with \(9\) of rank \(6\) (Proposition 5.3), and at order \(2^{11}\) there are \(9\) of rank \(7\), while direct generation at rank \(8\) finds none (below).

Checks. The case \(d=8\) (then \(c=4\), \(|P_3(Q)|=4\) and \(P_4(Q)=\langle n\rangle\), as in the first paragraph of the proof) was first settled through \(V=Q/P_3(Q)\), of order \(2^9\), rank \(8\) and \(2\)-class \(2\): \(R=Q/\langle n\rangle\) is an immediate descendant of step \(1\) of \(V\), of class \(2\) by Remark 5.5(ii) (if it had class \(3\), then \(d+4e_R+2\le11\) with \(e_R\ge1\), i.e. \(d\le5\)). In the SmallGroups library the groups of order \(2^9\) and rank \(8\) are the \(12\) groups SmallGroup\((512,i)\), \(10\,494\,201\le i\le10\,494\,212\) (a group \(V\) of rank \(n\) with \(|\Phi(V)|=2\) is determined by its squaring map \(q\colon V/\Phi(V)\to\Phi(V)\), a nonzero quadratic form on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) whose polar form is the commutator form, so such groups correspond to nonzero quadratic forms up to equivalence; if the polar form has rank \(2k\) and radical \(R\), then \(q|_R=0\) gives two classes for each \(1\le k\le n/2\) (Arf invariant \(0\) or \(1\)) and \(q|_R\ne0\) one class for each \(0\le k<n/2\), so \(2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+\lceil n/2\rceil\) classes, \(12\) for \(n=8\); the same formula gives the numbers of groups of order \(2^{n+1}\) and rank \(n\) in SmallGroups for \(n=2,\dots,7\), namely \(3,4,6,7,9,10\)). Of the \(11\) non-abelian ones, \(10\) have trivial nucleus and hence no immediate descendants at all [OBr90]; for SmallGroup\((512,10\,494\,202)\) the nucleus has dimension \(1\), but every immediate descendant of class \(\le3\) has class \(3\), so it has no descendant \(R\) of class \(2\). Both are read off the \(p\)-covering group, without computing automorphism groups; the two rules, with proofs by hand, are in compute/pq2048/README.md (Rules \(0\) and \(2\)), where they are also checked against full ANUPQ expansion. The remaining group SmallGroup\((512,10\,494\,201)\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\) is excluded by Lemma 5.6.

An independent check of rank \(8\) by direct generation agrees: on \(\mathbb{Z}/4\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^7\) the unmodified ANUPQ needs an estimated \(20\) GB of memory, while a version with reduced memory use completes it in \(2.1\) GB, finding \(8\) immediate descendants of order \(2^{10}\); the walk from all \(12\) groups then gives no candidate of order \(2^{11}\).

Central products. A search beyond order \(2^{11}\) may skip candidates that split as central products with a small factor. Let \(E\) be a finite \(2\)-group of class \(2\) with \(E/Z(E)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2\) and cyclic centre. Replacing \(E\) by the subgroup generated by two lifts \(a,b\) of a basis of \(E/Z(E)\), which does not change the central product below, one has \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8\}\) or \(E\cong M_{2^{k+2}}=\langle a,b\mid a^{2^{k+1}}=b^2=1,\ a^b=a^{1+2^k}\rangle\), \(k\ge2\), with \(Z(E)=\langle a^2\rangle\) (an elementary verification, which we omit). For an embedding \(\varphi\colon Z(E)\to Z(H)\) let \(H\circ E=(H\times E)/\{(\varphi(z),z^{-1})\}\), \(t=\varphi([a,b])\) and, for \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(s=\varphi(a^2)\).

Proposition. Let \(H\) be a group with \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\), and \(n\ge2\). • If \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8\}\), then \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\). • If \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\) and for some \(g\in H\) the element \(c=g^{-2}s\) satisfies \(c^{2^j}-1\in\Delta(H)^{j+2}\) for all \(j\ge0\) (for instance \(c^{2^j}\in\gamma_{j+2}(H)\)), then \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\). This holds in particular if \(s=g^2\) for some \(g\in H\), central or not (\(c=1\)), and if \(s\in\gamma_2(H)\), \(s^2\in\gamma_3(H)\) (\(g=1\), \(k=2\)).
Proof. (The proposition is also formally verified, in a slightly different form, see §4.)

Let \(Q\ge H\) be one of the groups below, generated by \(H\) and elements commuting with \(H\), and \(\gamma_2(Q)=\gamma_2(H)\). Then \(D_n(Q)\subseteq\gamma_2(Q)\subseteq H\) and \(D_n(H)\subseteq D_n(Q)\), so \(D_n(Q)=D_n(H)\) follows once \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(Q)^n\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). For that it suffices to have a left \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\)-linear \(q\colon\mathbb{Z}[Q]\to\mathbb{Z}[H]\), the identity on \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\), with \(q(\Delta(Q)^n)\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). Here \(\gamma_2(H\circ E)=\gamma_2(H)\langle t\rangle=\gamma_2(H)\).

(1) Let \(E=D_8\), \(c=[a,b]\), \(\tau=c-1\) (so \(\tau^2=-2\tau\)), and \(N=\mathbb{Z}[E/\langle b\rangle]\), free over \(\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]\) on \(e_0\) and \(f=ae_0-e_0\). Then \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]}N\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}[Q]\)-module, and \(q(u)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes p)(u(1\otimes e_0))\) with \(p(xe_0+yf)=x\) is as required. Indeed, \(\Delta(Q)^n\) is spanned by products of \(i\) factors from \(\Delta(H)\) and \(n-i\) from \(\Delta(E)\), and on \(N\) in the coordinates \((x,y)\) one has \(a-1\colon(x,y)\mapsto(0,x-2y)\) and \(b-1\colon(x,y)\mapsto(\tau y,\tau y)\). By induction, \(p(\Delta(E)^jN)=\tau^{\lceil j/2\rceil}\mathbb{Z}[\langle c\rangle]\) for \(j\ge1\); as \(t-1\in\Delta(H)^2\), \(q(\Delta(Q)^n)\subseteq\sum_i\Delta(H)^i(t-1)^{\lceil(n-i)/2\rceil}\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\). For \(Q_8\): \(u=ab\in D_8\) has \(u^2=t\), so \(H'=H\langle u\rangle\le H\circ D_8\) and \(D_n(H')=D_n(H)\). If \(a',b'\) are the generators of the factor \(D_8\) of \(H'\circ D_8\), the elements \(a'u,b'u\) generate a \(Q_8\) meeting \(H'\) in \(\langle t\rangle\), so \(H\circ Q_8\le H'\circ D_8\) and \(D_n(H\circ Q_8)\subseteq D_n(H')\cap H=D_n(H)\), using (1) for \(H'\).

(2) Let \(H''=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r\) central, \(r^2=s\), \(\langle r\rangle\cap H=\langle s\rangle\). With \(a',b'\) the generators of the factor \(D_8\) of \(H''\circ D_8\), the elements \(a'r,b'\) generate a copy of \(E\) meeting \(H''\) in \(\langle s\rangle\), and \(H\langle a\rangle\cong H''\) inside \(H\circ E\); by (1), \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H'')\). Now \(\mathbb{Z}[H'']=\mathbb{Z}[H]\oplus\mathbb{Z}[H]r\); put \(q(u_0+u_1r)=u_0+u_1g\). As \(r\) is central, \(\Delta(H'')^n=\sum_i\Delta(H)^{n-i}(r-1)^i\mathbb{Z}[H'']\), so it suffices that \(f_i=q((r-1)^i)\in\Delta(H)^i\) for all \(i\). In the abelian group \(\langle g,s,r\rangle\) put \(y=rg^{-1}\), so \(y^2=c\), and \(x=g-1\), \(\eta=y-1\), \(\tau=c-1\). Then \(r-1=x+\eta+x\eta\) and \(f_i=\sum_{\alpha+\beta\ge i}m_{\alpha\beta}\,x^\alpha e_\beta\) with \(e_b=\pi(\eta^b)\), \(\pi(v_0+v_1y)=v_0+v_1\). From \(\eta^2=\tau-2\eta\) we get \(e_1=0\), \(e_2=\tau\) and \(e_{b+2}=\tau e_b-2e_{b+1}\). The identity \(2(c^{2^j}-1)=(c^{2^{j+1}}-1)-(c^{2^j}-1)^2\) and the hypothesis give \(2^m\tau\in\Delta(H)^{m+2}\) for all \(m\). Hence, by induction on \(b\ge1\), \(2^me_b\in\Delta(H)^{b+m}\) for all \(m\); in particular \(e_b\in\Delta(H)^b\).

The condition \(c\in\gamma_2(H)\), i.e. \(s\in\Phi(H)\) for a \(2\)-group, cannot be dropped from the method: if \(s\notin\Phi(H)\), no such \(q\) for \(H''\) satisfies \(q(\Delta(H'')^2)\subseteq\Delta(H)^2\). Indeed, \((r-1)^2=(s-1)-2(r-1)\) would give \((s-1)-2x\in\Delta(H)^2\) with \(x=q(r)-1\); applying the augmentation shows \(x\in\Delta(H)\), so \(s-1\in2\Delta(H)+\Delta(H)^2\), i.e. \(s\in H^2\gamma_2(H)=\Phi(H)\). A computation shows that for the \(386\) candidates \(H\) of orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\), \(t=n\in\gamma_3(H)\). The \(291\) with \(|Z(H)|\ge8\) have \(s\) a square in the cyclic \(Z(H)\). Of the \(95\) with \(Z(H)\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\), \(78\) have \(s\in\gamma_2(H)\) and \(s^2\in\gamma_3(H)\), and the other \(17\) have \(s=g^2\) with \(g\in H\) not central. So by Proposition 5.8, \(D_n(H\circ E)=D_n(H)\) for all of them, all \(n\) and \(E\in\{D_8,Q_8,M_{16}\}\). Independently, the lattice computation gives \(D_4=D_5=1\) for all \(1\,544\) such products.

Gluing along a proper subgroup. For \(C\le Z(E)\) and an embedding \(\varphi\colon C\to Z(H)\) let \(H\circ_CE=(H\times E)/\{(\varphi(z),z^{-1})\colon z\in C\}\). Then \(H'=HZ(E)\) centralises \(E\), \(H\circ_CE=H'\circ E\) is a gluing along all of \(Z(E)\) (with \(\varphi\) the inclusion, so \(s=a^2\in H'\) for \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\)), and \(\gamma_i(H')=\gamma_i(H)\) for \(i\ge2\). For \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(H'\circ E\) can be written as \(H\circ_CE\) with \(C\ne Z(E)\) exactly when \(s\notin\Phi(H')\), which is where the method of part (2) for \(H'\) fails by the remark above. The projection then has to go to \(H\) instead of \(H'\).

Lemma. Let \(K=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r\) central, \(|K:H|=m\), and \(r^m=\sigma=g^m\) for some \(g\in H\), not necessarily central. Then \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n=\Delta(H)^n\) for all \(n\), and \(D_n(K)=D_n(H)\) for \(n\ge2\).
Proof. (The lemma is also formally verified, §4.)

\(\mathbb{Z}[K]=\bigoplus_{0\le j<m}\mathbb{Z}[H]r^j\); put \(q(\sum_ju_jr^j)=\sum_ju_jg^j\). As \(r^m=g^m\in H\), \(q(ur^j)=ug^j\) for all \(j\in\mathbb{Z}\), so \(q(u\,p(r))=u\,p(g)\) for every Laurent polynomial \(p\). As \(r\) is central, \(\Delta(K)^n\) is spanned by the \(x(r-1)^ir^j\) with \(x\in\Delta(H)^{n-i}\), and \(q(x(r-1)^ir^j)=x(g-1)^ig^j\in\Delta(H)^n\). Hence \(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n=q(\mathbb{Z}[H]\cap\Delta(K)^n)\subseteq\Delta(H)^n\); the reverse inclusion is clear, and \(D_n(K)\subseteq\gamma_2(K)=\gamma_2(H)\subseteq H\) gives the rest.

For \(m=2\) this is the case \(c=1\) of Proposition 5.8(2). Let \(E=M_{2^{k+2}}\), \(C=\langle a^{2^{j+1}}\rangle\) with \(1\le j<k\), and \(\sigma=\varphi(a^{2^{j+1}})\). If \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\) and \(\sigma=g^{2^{j+1}}\) for some \(g\in H\), then \(D_n(H\circ_CE)=D_n(H)\) for \(n\ge2\): in the proof of (2) for \(H'\) one has \(H''=H'\langle r\rangle=H\langle r\rangle\) with \(r^{2^{j+1}}=\sigma\) and \(\langle r\rangle\cap H=\langle\sigma\rangle\), so \(|H'':H|=2^{j+1}\), and Lemma 5.9 applies with \(m=2^{j+1}\). For instance, \(H\circ_{\langle t\rangle}M_{16}\) needs \(t=g^4\). The hypothesis \(t\in\gamma_2(H)\) costs nothing for the search: if \(H\circ_CE\) is a candidate, \(t\) is the involution of its cyclic centre, so \(t=n\in\gamma_3(H\circ_CE)=\gamma_3(H)\). A computation shows that, of the \(386\) candidates of orders \(2^6\)–\(2^9\), \(20\) split as central products (\(5\) of order \(2^8\), \(15\) of order \(2^9\)), with \(212\) factors \(E\) in all. The gluing is proper in \(16\) of these splittings, belonging to \(4\) candidates, always with \(M_{32}\) or \(M_{64}\); Lemma 5.9 covers \(4\) of them. Each of the \(20\) candidates also has a splitting covered by Proposition 5.8, so at these orders a search that skips split candidates does not need proper gluing (code: compute/central). The other \(12\) splittings would need an analogue of (2) for \(m=4\) (taking \(H\) maximal in \(H'\), i.e. \(j=1\)) with \(g^{-4}\sigma\ne1\); it cannot go through a projection to \(H\) in general, since for \(Q=D_8\circ_{\langle t\rangle}M_{16}\) one has \(\mathbb{Z}[D_8]\cap\Delta(Q)^n\ne\Delta(D_8)^n\) at \(n=4,5\) (index \(4\)), although \(D_n(Q)=D_n(D_8)\) by computation. Whether such an analogue holds is open.
